panels.title: Daemon security and operational gotchas
panels.body:
Docker socket = root equivalent.
/var/run/docker.sock gives full daemon control — mounting it into a
container (e.g. for CI) is a privileged escalation vector. Use
authz plugins or a rootless daemon for multi-tenant hosts.

live-restore: true — containers keep running if dockerd restarts
or crashes. Essential for production; prevents accidental outages
during daemon upgrades. Off by default.

json-file without log rotation: the default log driver writes
unbounded JSON to disk. Prod hosts fill up. Always set max-size
and max-file in daemon.json or per-container --log-opt.

userns-remap: maps container root (UID 0) to a high host UID
(e.g. 100000). Container root writes appear as UID 100000 on host.
Breaks volume permissions unless you chown data dirs to the
mapped UID. Test before enabling in prod.

conflicting daemon.json vs CLI flags: dockerd fails to start if
the same option is set in both daemon.json and a systemd
ExecStart= flag. Check: journalctl -u docker.service

panels.title: Logging drivers
pros: json-file (default): works everywhere, no infrastructure needed; docker logs command works
fluentd / awslogs / gcplogs: streams directly to centralized log system; no disk fill risk on host
cons: json-file: fills disk without rotation; docker logs N/A for very old logs after rotation
Non-json-file drivers: docker logs command returns 'Error — configured logging driver does not support reading'
